blogTitle: How Do I Choose a Color Palette for Wall Art?
videoTitle: How Do I Choose a Color Palette for Wall Art?
script:
How Do I Choose a Color Palette for Wall Art?

[warmly] You know that feeling when you hang a piece of art you LOVED in the shop… and something just feels off at home? Yeah — it's almost always about colour.

Here's the thing… the very FIRST step is to stop looking at art and start looking at your room — your sofa, your rug, your curtains. Those are your brief.

Start by picking THREE anchor colours from your room — your wall colour, your biggest piece of furniture, and your floor or rug. Your art needs to share at LEAST one of those.

So from those anchors you pick ONE hero colour for the art, add a supporting tone, allow ONE small accent pop — and keep the whole palette to four colours MAX.

[excited] Honestly, a little trick I love: take a photo of your room, open any free editing app, use the colour picker — and you'll have your EXACT hex codes in five minutes.

Now — matching art to your room doesn't mean MATCHY-matchy… think of it like putting together an outfit. The pieces don't have to be identical, they just need to belong together.

My go-to is the 'pull and echo' method — you pull ONE colour from something already in the room, like a velvet cushion or a plant pot, and echo it in the art… even a small area of that colour is ENOUGH.

When it comes to popular palette STYLES — you've got monochromatic, analogous, and complementary… each one gives a totally different mood, you know?

A tried-and-tested favourite? Teal sofa, burnt orange accent, cream wall art… it sounds bold but the warm undertones in the floor PULL it all together — trust me.

[curious] Colour theory sounds a bit technical… but honestly, the basics are SIMPLE — complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel and create contrast, analogous colours sit next to each other and feel calm.

The 60-30-10 RULE is your best friend here — 60 percent dominant colour, 30 percent secondary, 10 percent accent. It keeps everything balanced without being boring.

Room by ROOM it really does change — living rooms love warm neutrals and a bold anchor; bedrooms want softer, more tonal palettes; bathrooms suit botanicals and spa-like greens…

And this is a perfect example for a BATHROOM — soft florals, shabby chic tones, a little blush and sage… it's calm, it's fresh, and it makes the whole room feel considered.

If you're not sure where to start, a colour palette GENERATOR tool — there are free ones everywhere — lets you upload a photo of your room and it spits out the exact tones already in your space.

A little tip I love: once you have your palette from the tool, search for art using THOSE tones as your filter — it saves so much second-guessing, and a lot of returning and re-ordering…

When you're mixing MULTIPLE pieces — a gallery wall, a set of three — the key is a shared palette across all of them, even if the subjects are completely different.

Here's a great example — this abstract blue, pink and gold set works as a collection because all THREE prints share the same tonal palette… it feels curated, not random.

[warmly] And a simple tip for a cohesive multi-piece collection — pick one FRAME colour across all the pieces. Even if the art itself varies, that shared frame ties everything together beautifully.

And THIS set is a beautiful example of that — three prints, same frame, different compositions, completely cohesive… it just WORKS as a wall.

Now for 2024 to 2025 — the colour trends we're seeing are warm terracottas, dusty sage, deep moody plums, and a lot of nature-inspired earthy OCHRES… it's all about warmth and groundedness.

And honestly — this designer set is very much in that 2024-2025 moment… warm, grounded, works beautifully in a living room that wants a bit of DEPTH without going dark.

One thing people don't think about enough — the FINISH of your art changes how the colour reads… matte prints absorb light and feel softer, canvas adds texture, gloss makes colours pop more.

[softly] In a room with lots of natural light, a matte or canvas finish keeps things calm and WARM — in a darker room, a little gloss or metallic can really lift the colour without changing the palette.

For pure visual inspiration — something like this cherry blossom set is a GREAT example of colour done right… soft blush, dusty sage, warm white… it's calming, it's beautiful, and it works in so many rooms.

And this set — I love this one — the palette carries that same calm energy but with a bit more STRUCTURE… it's the kind of wall art that makes a room feel like someone actually THOUGHT about it.

One last thing worth knowing — your wall COLOUR matters more than people think… a warm cream wall shifts every colour warmer; a cool grey wall shifts everything cooler. TEST your art in your actual light before committing.

[warmly] So to bring it all together — start with your room's existing colours, build a palette of two to FOUR tones, use the 60-30-10 rule, and choose art that belongs in that system… and the whole room lifts.
